planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Cheyenne bears young and needs a Type II pollinator such as Elliott or Desirable, and its compact size suits closer spacing than many standard pecan cultivars.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Released by the USDA breeding program, Cheyenne is notable for its smaller, more compact tree size compared to many pecan cultivars, along with excellent kernel quality and a high percentage of kernel to shell. It tends to bear at a younger age than older heirloom cultivars, giving growers an earlier return on a new planting, though it is more susceptible to pecan scab in humid climates and benefits from good spacing and airflow. Its compact habit makes it a reasonable option where space is more limited than a full commercial pecan grove requires.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pecan Variety Selection

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Mahan produces some of the largest pecan nuts of any cultivar but has a lower kernel percentage and is more prone to alternate bearing than modern selections.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. One of the earliest widely planted named pecan cultivars, dating to the early 1900s, Mahan is known for producing exceptionally large nuts, among the biggest of any pecan cultivar, though the kernel fill and disease resistance lag behind modern breeding selections. It remains of historical interest and is still grown in some older orchards and by collectors of heirloom pecan varieties for its striking nut size, even though it has largely been superseded commercially by higher-yielding, more scab-resistant cultivars.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pecan Variety Selection
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Pecan Varieties

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Moreland shows good resistance to pecan scab, an important trait in the humid Gulf South, and needs a Type I pollinator.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Selected for reliable production and notably good resistance to pecan scab, a fungal disease that is a major limiting factor for pecan growing in humid Gulf Coast climates, Moreland has long been a dependable choice for growers in Louisiana, Mississippi, and neighboring states where less resistant cultivars require heavy fungicide programs. Nuts are medium-sized with good kernel quality, and the tree is a consistent annual bearer under good management, making it a solid choice for growers prioritizing lower-input disease tolerance over maximum nut size.
sources: LSU AgCenter — Commercial Pecan Production in Louisiana
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pecan Variety Selection
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Pecan Varieties

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Success is an older cultivar that is more disease-prone than modern selections and benefits from a fungicide program in humid regions.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Introduced in the early 1900s, Success was among the important early named pecan cultivars that helped establish the commercial pecan industry in the South, valued in its day for good nut size and quality. It has largely been replaced in modern commercial orchards by more disease-resistant, higher-yielding cultivars, since it is fairly susceptible to pecan scab and other diseases common in humid climates, but it remains of historical interest and is still found in older plantings and heirloom nut collections.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pecan Variety Selection
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Pecan Varieties

common_name: Western Schley Pecan (Widely Planted Southwestern Irrigated Pecan)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Western Schley is one of the most widely planted pecan cultivars in irrigated Southwestern orchards and needs a Type II pollinator such as Desirable or Elliott.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety, and provide consistent irrigation during nut fill, since this cultivar was developed for and performs best under the irrigated growing conditions of the arid Southwest. Often simply called Western in the trade, it produces a thin-shelled, well-filled nut with good flavor and has become one of the most heavily planted commercial pecan cultivars in New Mexico, Arizona, and West Texas orchards. It shows somewhat better tolerance of drier climates than many Southeastern-bred cultivars but still performs acceptably in the more humid Gulf South when given good air circulation and disease management.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pecan Variety Selection
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Pecan Varieties
